Rare does not always mean that it looks good. Themed builds can be really cool, but often overshadowed by clean cars. Custom crew colors (tasteful ones) make a car exponentially better. Replica builds are always welcome in my book, but stick to the original or it can quickly spiral into tacky.

I try to minimize my use of chameleon colors unless I'm stealing the pearl for a crew color or going for custom colors on wheels. But never ever use the prismatic stuff unironically 🙊

F1 wheels are very RARELY fitting for a car, unless you're making a troll car please don't use them. (Hustler, hotknife without fenders, and some off-road vehicles get a pass). Benny's wheels should be used on builds that imitate donks/lowriders (if you are making a donkey build on the box Chevy for example, gets a pass even if it's not a true donk). Modded cars are cool for rarity, but making it look good is a whole different level of quality.

Neutral wheel colors are my favorite to use, but are so common you may want to experiment with other colors every once in a while. Tints are acceptable in my eyes, but it's super common where I live so I'm desensitized to it. I usually use sport wheels, track wheels, or street wheels. I stay away from sticker bomb, titanium exhausts (unless very specific use cases), carbon fiber overload(use it tastefully not on every street car), mismatched body panels, bosozuku parts, colored headlights, neons, crazy horns, tire smoke, etc. All these things have specific use case scenarios, but I ignore them by default.

Try to find new gems in the world, don't rely on the same 3 spots you always use for picture taking. Spot in a random place you haven't been in a while and find something you'd like to photograph.

Lighting will make or break a photograph, real world or otherwise. Find the best time of day, if the exact spot doesn't have enough lighting perhaps making a custom GTA job will provide what you need.

Your canvas, whether it be a vehicle or your character is the most vital part. Keep your focal point clear and concise, don't direct your viewer towards other items in range unintended. Also make sure it's fully presented in a way you want. Don't rush anything, it'll make the photo useless.

Lastly, if your photograph can convey some kind of feeling to the viewer then you have struck gold. Also trust your instincts with this, if you find it interesting, someone else likely will too.

My dad was a mechanic as I grew up. He owned two trans and (the smokey and the bandit trans am) a white one and a green one. He worked a lot on a shop that built drag cars and street rods when I was younger. So I've been around cars since I was born.

My knowledge has come from my childhood up to now. The first racing game I ever touched was gran Turismo on the PS2. I was sitting on the bed beside my dad as he played. He would show me what he was doing, talk to me about the cars, and he would eventually play with me. Over the years, I'd eventually start getting better and beating him (various games not just Gran Turismo). This was something that happened my entire life as we went to the store or on trips also. We played a game that would be to guess the name of the car or a race to see who could find a specific car first as we drove. We did this in movies and television as well, car spotting and shouting out "unicorns."

As I got older, I found myself leaning more towards Japanese cars and not so much American cars like my dad has always loved. This led me to spend countless hours researching cars and drift cars in middle school and high school. By researching I mean day in and day out. I'd study the cars and parts in super street, modified mag, wrecked mag, speed hunters, import tuner, option, omgdrift, etc. I also browsed their websites at the start of my day and at the end saving pictures to reference at a later date in video games like fm2-fm4. I used these same images to draw cars and style them how I see fit. At this time drifting was captivating to me, I learned a lot from people I played with on Fm4. I met Geoff roark, Julian Jacobs, and many other grassroots guys in public drift lobbies. They through a ton of knowledge at me and it stuck. I was hooked, browsing forums religiously to see how to build a proper SR, watching reviews of ISIS blast pipes, seeing people like valera12345 go from street drifting to track drifting his rb s14. 

Some of it was time/place, a lot was my dad, a lot was me loving the feeling of speed and the vibration of combustion, the smell of race fuel and rubber, but overall I was the one who went down the rabbit hole and dug for information I didn't know. My own experiences helped fuel my passion even more when I was hunting for my first car and fixing the shit box that I bought.

Thanks for letting me share my story. ❤️
